mensaje_crack.cuerpo:
Nathan,

Two weeks ago I asked how long it takes one of your dock supervisors to get last week's dwell time. I'll guess: about a day, and usually wrong — that is what the COO of a 14-warehouse distributor told me yesterday.

At a 200-person plant in Monterrey that number went from 40 minutes to 6, with the supervisors doing it themselves. The difference was not the software: we trained the tool on how each supervisor already reports, instead of training the supervisors on the tool.

If dock scheduling is still the thing you post about, 15 minutes next week and I'll show you exactly what we did. If not, this is my last note.

Pablo González
Bentley University · VYNMSA

mensaje_crack.asunto: What to promise a sawmill that asks for AI
mensaje_crack.cuerpo:
Alain,

You wrote that every sawmill customer asks you for AI and you don't know what to promise. I'd promise them one thing: the inspection report their shift lead already writes, done in six minutes instead of forty.

That is what we did at a 200-person metal-parts plant in Monterrey: 31 of 38 supervisors use the assistant every week, because it was trained on how they report, not the other way around. Your cameras already see the board; the missing piece is the sentence the shift lead writes about it.

If you want, 15 minutes next week and I'll show you how it was scoped. I'm in Boston; Montreal is a short flight if it ever makes sense.

Pablo González
Bentley University · VYNMSA

borradores.post:
A founder asked me yesterday to explain AI "without the hype". Here is the whole thing in one line: AI adapts to the worker, not the worker to AI. That is the difference between automating and amplifying.

At a 200-person plant in Monterrey, five planners went from two days to four hours on customer orders. No new software. The same people, with an assistant that learned their spreadsheets.

If your team is afraid of the tool, you bought the wrong tool.
borradores.huella: AI adapts to the worker, not the worker to AI
